name: Cobalt Kitty Campaign
desc: Cobalt Kitty campaign conducted by OceanLotus.

acts.d: Link to a malicious site that downloads a fake Flash Installer delivering Cobalt Strike beacon.
Word documents with malicious macros downloading Cobalt Strike payloads
Two scheduled tasks are created that download additional payloads
Obfuscated PowerShell scripts delivering Cobalt Strike beacons are downloaded
Obfuscated and XOR'ed PowerShell is decoded to download additional obfuscated PowerShell payloads
Obfuscated PowerShell scripts that executes a Cobalt Strike beacon
Attackers dropped Visual Basic and PowerShell scripts in folders that they created under the ProgramData
Windows Registry Autorun is used to execute VBScript and PowerShell scripts residing in the ProgramData folder
Payloads for persistence were hidden in NTFS Alternate Data Streams
Scheduled tasks are created that load malicious PowerShell payloads using DLL hijacking with a Google Update binary
Windows services were created and/or modified to load PowerShell scripts
Malicious Outlook backdoor macros were to used to communicate with C2 servers and exfiltrate data
A malicious DLL file was implanted where the Windows Search Service would run and load the DLL
Regsvr32.exe is used to download COM scriplets for malicious execution
Cobalt Strike's malleable C2 profiles were used to impersonate Amazon, Google Safe Browsing, Pandora, and OSCP traffic
DNS tunneling was used for C2 communication and data exfiltration
Malicious Outlook macros were created to utilize email for C2 communication and data exfiltration
Network scanning was performed against entire ranges to gain information on open ports, services, and operating systems for remote systems
The attackers used several tools built into the Windows OS to gather information on the environment’s users.
Network scanning was performed against entire ranges to gain information on open ports, services, and operating systems
The attackers used several tools built into the Windows OS to gather information on the environment’s network configurations.
The attackers used several tools built into the Windows OS to gather information on the environment’s network connections.
Modified version of Mimikatz was used to dump credentials
Net.exe was used to perform lateral movement via Windows Admin Shares
WMI and 'net user' commands were used to deploy tools on remote machines
The attackers deployed a customized Mimikatz using stolen credentials from an administrative account, which they used to carry out a pass-the-hash attack
The attackers deployed a customized Mimikatz using stolen credentials from an administrative account, which they used to carry out a pass-the-ticket attack
